key_insight: Vision-language models increasingly prioritize textual prompts over visual evidence as object count rises, leading them to conform to incorrect prompt assertions (prompt-induced hallucination) even when the image contradicts the prompt.
problem_solved: Characterizes when and why VLMs hallucinate by following overstated prompts in an object-counting setting, isolating the prompt vs. visual-evidence tradeoff.
method: Controlled object-counting experiments where prompts overstate the number of objects (e.g., ask for four when three are present) to isolate prompt influence.
Systematic evaluation across varying object counts to measure the transition from prompt-correction to prompt-conformity.
Mechanistic analysis of failure modes (e.g., dominance of language priors vs. weakened visual grounding) to explain prompt-induced hallucination.
impact: Provides practical insight for diagnosing and reducing prompt-induced hallucinations in VLMs, informing prompt design, evaluation protocols, and model training strategies to improve visual grounding and reliability.
visual_elements: Bar chart: prompt-conformity rate vs. true object count (shows rising conformity with higher counts).
Side-by-side example panel: input image + overstating prompt → model outputs (correct count vs. hallucinated response).
Mechanism diagram: competing influence of textual prompt and visual evidence as object count increases.
Attention/activation heatmap or schematic illustrating weakened visual grounding when prompts assert specific counts.
paper_title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
paper_authors: William Rudman, Michal Golovanevsky, Dana Arad, Yonatan Belinkov, Ritambhara Singh
